name: Simeon Solomon
teaser: The Pre-Raphaelite prodigy who fell — a Jewish painter of androgynous angels and biblical lovers, celebrated at 18, then destroyed by scandal and addiction. His angels still glow with a beauty that cost him everything.

exploreAction.targetName: The Angel of Death or the Jewish wedding scenes
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the face of the Angel of Death: not a skeleton but a beautiful, mournful youth. Solomon painted sacred figures with a tenderness that was radical for its time. He was the darling of the Pre-Raphaelites at 18; by 30 he was homeless. The angels survived his fall.

name: Arthur Hughes
teaser: The gentlest of the Pre-Raphaelites — his paintings of children, gardens, and lovers are painted with a tenderness that made him one of the most loved Victorian illustrators. His April Love and The Long Engagement are icons of wistful romance.

exploreAction.targetName: April Love (Tate Britain) — the couple
exploreAction.instruction: A young woman and her lover in a wood, her face half-turned away — the title is a pun: it's April, and it's about love that may not last. Look at the flowers, the falling petals, the yearning. Hughes painted the moment before a sentence is spoken, and made it eternal.

name: Henry Wallis
teaser: The Pre-Raphaelite painter of a single masterpiece — Chatterton, the death of the young poet, is one of the most famous images in British art. Its model, George Meredith, later married and abandoned the painter's wife in a scandal.

exploreAction.targetName: Chatterton (Tate Britain) — the pose
exploreAction.instruction: A young poet lies dead on a bed, poison vial in hand, morning light through the window, a torn poem at his feet. Look at the composition — the body arranged like a fallen statue, the garret of 1770 rendered with 1856 accuracy. Wallis painted one perfect thing and spent the rest of his career living in its shadow.

name: John William Waterhouse
teaser: The late Pre-Raphaelite of mythic women — his Lady of Shalott, Ophelia, and Circe are among the most reproduced images of Victorian art. He painted doomed beauties at the edge of water, and made death look like a dream.

exploreAction.targetName: The Lady of Shalott (Tate Britain) — the boat
exploreAction.instruction: The lady floats downriver to Camelot in her boat, the tapestry half-unraveled around her, the candles guttering out. Look at the symbolism: her curse was to see the world only in a mirror, and she broke it for love. Waterhouse painted the moment she chose to die looking.

name: William Holman Hunt
teaser: The most earnest of the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood — he painted with such literal intensity that he traveled to the Holy Land to paint Jerusalem and the Dead Sea from life. The Light of the World is among the most famous religious images in the world.

exploreAction.targetName: The Light of the World (Keble College, Oxford) — the door
exploreAction.instruction: Christ stands at a door with no handle, lantern in hand, knocking — the handle is on the inside, because only you can open it. Look at the overgrown ivy, the starry night, the patient face. Hunt painted it three times; it toured the world and millions queued to see it.

name: Richard Dadd
teaser: The Victorian painter who killed his father and spent 42 years in an asylum — where he painted The Fairy Feller's Master-Stroke, an impossibly detailed fantasy of a fairy woodcutter, watched by every creature of folklore. It is obsession made beautiful.

exploreAction.targetName: The Fairy Feller's Master-Stroke (Tate Britain) — the details
exploreAction.instruction: Stand close and look for the individual creatures: the fairy with the hatchet, the gnomes, the beetle, the face in the foliage — all painted under the delusion that a fairy ordered it. Dadd worked on it for nine years in Bedlam. The madness is in the precision; the beauty is in the madness.

name: William Quiller Orchardson
teaser: The Scottish painter of the grand Victorian interior — his scenes of aristocratic marriage, betrayal, and society are staged like theater, full of silence and implication. He painted the drawing room as a battlefield.

exploreAction.targetName: Her Mother's Voice or The First Cloud — the staging
exploreAction.instruction: Look at The First Cloud: a newlywed couple sits at opposite ends of a room, the first quarrel hanging in the air between them. Orchardson left the space between his figures empty on purpose — the emptiness is the subject. Society drama, told in furniture and silence.

name: Luke Fildes
teaser: The Victorian painter of social conscience — his Applicants for Admission to a Casual Ward exposed the poorhouse queues that polite London ignored. He later became the king of royal portraiture; his portrait of Edward VII is the official image of the king.

exploreAction.targetName: Applicants for Admission to a Casual Ward (Tate Britain) — the queue
exploreAction.instruction: A queue of the homeless and desperate waits outside a workhouse in the rain — a woman with a baby, a man with a bandaged head. Fildes painted it after visiting a real night-shelter, and it shocked Britain into debate. Then compare his royal portraits: the same painter, a different world.

name: Hubert von Herkomer
teaser: The German-born Victorian painter of labor and grief — his Hard Times shows a family of travelling workers resting by the roadside, and his monumental portraits of workers made him one of Britain's best-paid artists. He also founded his own art school.

exploreAction.targetName: Hard Times (Manchester Art Gallery) — the family
exploreAction.instruction: A labourer and his children sit by the road, the mother asleep on a bank, a newspaper with 'hard times' headlines at their feet. Look at the faces — tired, quiet, dignified. Herkomer painted the new poor of industrial Britain without melodrama, and Victorian audiences recognized them at once.

name: Frank Holl
teaser: The Victorian painter of bereavement — his scenes of mourning, widowhood, and deathbeds made him the most sought-after painter of grief in England. He died at 43, exhausted by the success he never wanted.

exploreAction.targetName: Newgate: Committed for Trial or the mourning scenes
exploreAction.instruction: Look at Newgate: a prisoner parts from his family in the prison chapel, the clergyman between them, the light falling on the bars. Holl painted grief with a raw honesty that made fashionable society uncomfortable — and then they bought it anyway. He said he wanted to paint 'the real thing.'

name: George Clausen
teaser: The British painter of rural light — his farm workers, school girls, and cottage gardens are painted with an Impressionist brightness that brought French methods to English fields. He was the leading figure of British Impressionism.

exploreAction.targetName: The Stone Gatherers or the harvest scenes
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the light on the field: Clausen painted the English countryside with a French eye — bright, broken color, figures dissolved into sunlight. He grew up in poverty and painted farm work from memory and love. His fields are the most luminous in British art.

name: Stanhope Forbes
teaser: The founder of the Newlyn School — he settled in the Cornish fishing village of Newlyn and painted its fishermen, women, and weather with a serious, French-trained realism. He was called 'the father of British Impressionism.'

exploreAction.targetName: A Fish Sale on a Cornish Beach — the crowd
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the fish auction on the beach: buyers, sellers, and boats against the grey Cornish light. Forbes painted the scene on the spot, in the open air, with the villagers as his models. He stayed in Newlyn for 60 years and made it an artists' colony. One village, one painter, one endless sea.

name: Walter Langley
teaser: The Newlyn School painter of fisherfolk's hard lives — his scenes of mending nets, waiting for boats, and mourning lost husbands are painted with a social conscience rare in Victorian art. He was the school's most compassionate eye.

exploreAction.targetName: The Never, Never Land or the women waiting scenes
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the women: knitting, watching the sea, waiting for men who may not come back. Langley painted the cost of the fishing life — the grief behind the picturesque. He was a working-class Birmingham boy who painted Cornwall's poor with love, not distance.

name: Henry Scott Tuke
teaser: The Newlyn painter of summer boys and swimming light — his sunlit studies of youths diving, sailing, and resting on the Cornish coast are painted with a freedom that looks decades ahead of its time. He also painted portraits of a young soldier he loved.

exploreAction.targetName: The Bathers or the sailing scenes — the light
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the light on skin and water: Tuke painted his models out of doors, in real sun, with a freedom Victorian studios never allowed. His bathers are joyful, unselfconscious, and painted with total warmth. He was also a war artist; the same eye that loved the light documented its cost.

name: William Nicholson
teaser: The British painter of still lifes and posters — his lacquered jugs, bowls of fruit, and country views are painted with a flat, graphic clarity that made him a father of modern British art. He also designed some of the most famous posters ever made.

exploreAction.targetName: The silver jug still lifes or the country views
exploreAction.instruction: Look at how Nicholson flattens a jug and a bowl of apples: the objects read as shapes first, things second — a century before it was fashionable. Then find his posters — bold, black-and-white, unforgettable. He painted with a designer's eye and a painter's heart.

name: Walter Sickert
teaser: The British painter of the dingy and the true — his Camden Town nudes, music-hall scenes, and gritty interiors are painted with a deliberately 'ugly' honesty that made him the father of modern British painting. He also claimed — probably falsely — to be Jack the Ripper.

exploreAction.targetName: The Camden Town nudes or the music-hall scenes
exploreAction.instruction: Look at how Sickert paints a naked woman on an iron bed in a rented room: no idealization, just truth — a body, a room, a city's grime. He learned from Degas and taught the next century to look without flinching. He also loved to gossip and lied about being a murderer; his paintings are honest, his stories were not.

name: Duncan Grant
teaser: The Bloomsbury painter of decorative joy — his still lifes, portraits, and murals are full of bright, loose color and a playful sensuality. He lived for decades with the writer Lytton Strachey's family and helped define the look of English modernism.

exploreAction.targetName: The still lifes or the murals of the Borough Polytechnic
exploreAction.instruction: Look at how Grant makes a table of fruit sing: broad strokes, unexpected colors, the joy of paint itself. His murals for the Borough Polytechnic — scenes of sport and idleness — were scandalous in 1911 and are treasures now. He painted pleasure, seriously.

name: Vanessa Bell
teaser: The Bloomsbury painter and Virginia Woolf's sister — her portraits, still lifes, and interiors are painted with a bold, decorative modernism that made her the center of the group. She was also a brilliant designer of fabrics and book jackets.

exploreAction.targetName: The portraits of the Bloomsbury circle or the still lifes
exploreAction.instruction: Look at how Bell simplifies a face into blocks of color — her portrait of her sister Virginia is a study in affection and geometry. Then her designs: fabrics and dust jackets with the same confident shapes. She said she wanted to 'make things beautiful' — and she did, in every medium she touched.

name: Mark Gertler
teaser: The British painter of tragic intensity — his Merry-Go-Round, a circle of painted soldiers, is one of the great anti-war images of WWI. He burned with love for the painter Carrington (who chose Lytton Strachey), and died by suicide at 48.

exploreAction.targetName: The Merry-Go-Round (Tate Britain) — the soldiers
exploreAction.instruction: Soldiers ride a carousel painted like a machine of war — rigid, bright, and horrible, spinning nowhere. D.H. Lawrence called it 'the best modern painting.' Gertler painted his despair over unrequited love and a world at war into one spinning circle. Look long enough and it turns.

name: C.R.W. Nevinson
teaser: The British war artist who painted the trenches with a Cubist-Futurist machine aesthetic — his soldiers look like parts of a vast, doomed machine. He painted the front from the front, and it changed him forever.

exploreAction.targetName: La Mitrailleuse (Tate) — the machine gun
exploreAction.instruction: A machine-gun team in the trenches, drawn with angles and metal — the men and their weapon fused into one mechanism. Look at the faces: grey, blank, interchangeable. Nevinson painted war as industry. He called his style 'the art of machinery.' The machinery is eating the men.

name: Paul Nash
teaser: The British surrealist of the wounded landscape — his We Are Making a New World turns a WWI battlefield into a cold, cosmic dawn, and his later landscapes of roots, moons, and stones are England seen as a dream. He painted war's aftermath better than anyone.

exploreAction.targetName: We Are Making a New World (Imperial War Museum) — the sun
exploreAction.instruction: A pale sun rises over a field of shell craters and broken trees — the title is bitter irony. Look at the coldness: no people, just the aftermath, and the sun indifferent. Nash painted the landscape as the casualty. His later, stranger works — rooted shapes, moonlit stones — made England look like another planet.
